import Mathlib

noncomputable section

/-!
# An explicit counterexample to the Jacobian conjecture

For the polynomial map `map` below, we verify:

* its Jacobian determinant is the nonzero constant `-2`;
* three distinct rational points have the same image.

Since the coefficients and the three points are rational, the collision also
holds after extending scalars to `ℂ`.
-/

namespace JacobianCounterexample

section Ring

variable {K : Type*} [Field K]

def P (x y z : K) : K :=
  (1 + x * y) ^ 3 * z + y ^ 2 * (1 + x * y) * (4 + 3 * x * y)

def Q (x y z : K) : K :=
  y + 3 * x * (1 + x * y) ^ 2 * z + 3 * x * y ^ 2 * (4 + 3 * x * y)

def R (x y z : K) : K :=
  2 * x - 3 * x ^ 2 * y - x ^ 3 * z

def map (v : K × K × K) : K × K × K :=
  (P v.1 v.2.1 v.2.2, Q v.1 v.2.1 v.2.2, R v.1 v.2.1 v.2.2)

/- The same three coordinate functions as formal multivariate polynomials. -/
open MvPolynomial

def pPoly : MvPolynomial (Fin 3) K :=
  (C 1 + X 0 * X 1) ^ 3 * X 2
    + X 1 ^ 2 * (C 1 + X 0 * X 1) * (C 4 + C 3 * X 0 * X 1)

def qPoly : MvPolynomial (Fin 3) K :=
  X 1 + C 3 * X 0 * (C 1 + X 0 * X 1) ^ 2 * X 2
    + C 3 * X 0 * X 1 ^ 2 * (C 4 + C 3 * X 0 * X 1)

def rPoly : MvPolynomial (Fin 3) K :=
  C 2 * X 0 - C 3 * X 0 ^ 2 * X 1 - X 0 ^ 3 * X 2

def polynomialMap : Fin 3 → MvPolynomial (Fin 3) K :=
  ![pPoly, qPoly, rPoly]

/- This is the Jacobian defined using `MvPolynomial.pderiv`, rather than by
writing down derivative formulae. -/
def formalJacobian : Matrix (Fin 3) (Fin 3) (MvPolynomial (Fin 3) K) :=
  fun i j ↦ pderiv j (polynomialMap i)

/- `jacobian x y z` is obtained by formally differentiating `P`, `Q`, and
`R` with respect to `x`, `y`, and `z`, respectively. -/
def jacobian (x y z : K) : Matrix (Fin 3) (Fin 3) K :=
  !![
    3 * y * (1 + x * y) ^ 2 * z
        + y ^ 3 * ((4 + 3 * x * y) + 3 * (1 + x * y)),
    3 * x * (1 + x * y) ^ 2 * z
        + 2 * y * (1 + x * y) * (4 + 3 * x * y)
        + x * y ^ 2 * ((4 + 3 * x * y) + 3 * (1 + x * y)),
    (1 + x * y) ^ 3;

    3 * (1 + x * y) ^ 2 * z
        + 6 * x * y * (1 + x * y) * z
        + 3 * y ^ 2 * (4 + 3 * x * y) + 9 * x * y ^ 3,
    1 + 6 * x ^ 2 * (1 + x * y) * z
        + 6 * x * y * (4 + 3 * x * y) + 9 * x ^ 2 * y ^ 2,
    3 * x * (1 + x * y) ^ 2;

    2 - 6 * x * y - 3 * x ^ 2 * z,
    -3 * x ^ 2,
    -x ^ 3]

/- Thus the displayed matrix really is the evaluation of the formal
Jacobian of the three polynomials. -/
theorem eval_formalJacobian (x y z : K) (i j : Fin 3) :
    eval ![x, y, z] (formalJacobian (K := K) i j) = jacobian x y z i j := by
  fin_cases i <;> fin_cases j <;>
    simp [formalJacobian, polynomialMap, pPoly, qPoly, rPoly, jacobian] <;>
    ring

theorem jacobian_det (x y z : K) :
    (jacobian x y z).det = -2 := by
  simp [jacobian, Matrix.det_fin_three]
  ring

theorem jacobian_det_ne_zero [CharZero K] (x y z : K) :
    (jacobian x y z).det ≠ 0 := by
  rw [jacobian_det]
  norm_num

end Ring

section Collision

def a : ℚ × ℚ × ℚ := (0, 0, -1 / 4)
def b : ℚ × ℚ × ℚ := (1, -3 / 2, 13 / 2)
def c : ℚ × ℚ × ℚ := (-1, 3 / 2, 13 / 2)
def target : ℚ × ℚ × ℚ := (-1 / 4, 0, 0)

theorem map_a : map a = target := by
  norm_num [map, P, Q, R, a, target]

theorem map_b : map b = target := by
  norm_num [map, P, Q, R, b, target]

theorem map_c : map c = target := by
  norm_num [map, P, Q, R, c, target]

theorem a_ne_b : a ≠ b := by
  norm_num [a, b]

theorem a_ne_c : a ≠ c := by
  norm_num [a, c]

theorem b_ne_c : b ≠ c := by
  norm_num [b, c]

theorem not_injective : ¬ Function.Injective (map : (ℚ × ℚ × ℚ) → ℚ × ℚ × ℚ) := by
  intro h
  exact a_ne_b (h (map_a.trans map_b.symm))

end Collision

end JacobianCounterexample

@Franklin Harding The Lean Zulip is probably not the best place for an extended discussion here about the proof or how it was found. Unfortunately, much of that discussion is on X. But here is a quick summary. I don't think we know how the original counterexample was found with Fable, but since then it has been recreated many times with Fable and GPT 5.6, often asking for proofs with explicit motivation. I don't think there is any indication that brute force was needed. I know of at least three proofs, some more motivated than others. I think some in the algebraic geometry community find that this was much easier in hindsight than realized, especially when looking at the more motivated proofs.

This github repo has a lot of details about all three proofs as well as links back to the original X posts. https://github.com/nasqret/jacobian-counterexample. Also, he has a visual guide here for the proofs: https://nasqret.github.io/jacobian-counterexample/ [Edit: Note that this repo and visual guide are clearly AI-generated, at least in part.]

Edit: By "three proofs", I guess I mean the original counterexample and two motivated, explicit constructions of that same counterexample.

And Terry Tao has some commentary here also motivating the construction more (building on some of the conversations on X): https://terrytao.wordpress.com/2026/07/21/a-digestion-of-the-jacobian-conjecture-counterexample/

At the very end of that blog post Terry links to his conversation with ChatGPT, doing this "digestion".

https://chatgpt.com/share/6a5fdc7a-d6f8-83e8-bbea-8deb42cfed56

@Jason Rute thanks for the reply, after posting here I was eventually able to find the HN post recreating the CoT, and it seems like at least in that case the model was shelling out to some CAS. I'm not one of the people saying "this could have been found by brute force." There's a difference between brute forcing the conjecture entirely and the model using CAS to verify algebra, or Z3 to find a witness for some small search space as part of the reasoning process, or Lean to verify some small self-contained lemma, etc. I'm just surprised there isn't more discussion about this because to me it's the interesting part. If the model didn't even use CAS and just reasoned purely in natural language, that would be especially insane.

I wouldn't be surprised if the original prompt contained something like "make sure to check your algebra using Sage," and in general it makes me wonder what can be accomplished if you encourage more tool use.

I have a $100/month ChatGPT subscription and have been using it (on its highest level) on a variety of research-level math questions over the past few months. If we are prepared to accept at face value what it tells me as it's thinking (probably a reasonable assumption, although of course it's possible that it will say that it's using a tool when it isn't), then it makes heavy use of tools when appropriate, even though I never explicitly prompt it to use tools. Based on this experience, I would be very surprised if Fable used no tools for the Jacobian conjecture, even if the prompt said nothing to encourage it to do so.

On the other hand, I've never seen it say that it's using Lean or any ITP to verify any of its internal calculations. I also don't recall it ever saying that it was using some kind of proprietary CAS, though maybe it has said that and I didn't notice (or have forgotten). My guess is that for the Jacobian conjecture, it used open-source tools such as SymPy.

I should also say that even on its highest level, ChatGPT does still sometimes make false mathematical statements, even when it's something that is easy to confirm/refute with a small calculation. So it's certainly not foolproof, and doesn't always use tools when it "should." Nevertheless, in my experience, this type of mistake is rare.

Timothy Chow said:

I should also say that even on its highest level, ChatGPT does still sometimes make false mathematical statements, even when it's something that is easy to confirm/refute with a small calculation. So it's certainly not foolproof, and doesn't always use tools when it "should." Nevertheless, in my experience, this type of mistake is rare.

Indeed, I have found the rate of such mistakes being rare, but the dramatically egregious nature of them kind of does a wash in terms of the expected value consideration. For things you know well, its pretty good as they are cheap to sanity test and catch, albeit mostly flabbergasting when it does make some absurd and seemingly uncharacteristic mistake out of nowhere.

One thing I will share, when Opus made a very bizarre mistake where it essentially skipped using a tool and made some stuff up.

I perhaps naively quizzed claude Fable about why or how that can happen, usually this doesn't lead anywhere useful, but this time it basically said something along the lines off:

If you have a session that is full of repetitive similar tasks, built up in the context, the repetitive nature can seemingly pattern match and glitch the AI out, where it assumes it does not need to do any extra work and provides a plausible generation instead of using a tool. Since in the context it sees such repetitiveness, that contextual noise weighs it down somehow.

I don't know the veracity of that, but it makes intuitive sense, and I did find switching or adjusting focus of sessions more maybe anecdotally helped.

For Lean, at least, I think there is an uncomfortable situation. Two things are probably both true: (1) One doesn't need Lean to solve most of the math problems being solved here by the frontier AI models. (2) Lean would help in the long run. It ensures final correctness. And for real long-running AI investigations, judicious use of Lean (say with heavy use of conditional results) might help to checkpoint intermediate results and avoid error propagation. But since (1) is true, I think many frontier labs are a bit cautious not to rely too much on Lean in their math-solving abilities. LLM-skeptics like Gary Marcus often cry "but did it use Lean" when presented with results such as the unit distance conjecture, and the model makers reply with "no, it shouldn't matter if it did use Lean, but no it didn't". (Not exact quotes, but pretty close.) It's a bit of a sad situation.

What is puzzling is not why the models sometimes make mathematical mistakes. What is puzzling is how they can perform high-level mathematical reasoning at all, given that they are not explicitly following any rules of logic. The starting point, remember, is a randomized next-token generator. Frontier models are a lot more than randomized next-token generators, but fundamentally, that is the starting point. Therefore the default expectation should be that in any attempt at a sustained argument, they should go off the rails sooner or later, probably sooner rather than later. Indeed, the fact that for many mathematical tasks, they need to use tools to achieve any kind of reliability, bears out this expectation. That they nevertheless are able to carry out sustained mathematical arguments without using an ITP as a tool is a minor miracle, which I don't think anybody understands. Algorithmic thinking theory seeks to analyze the phenomenon that feeding an LLM its own answers to a question, and repeating this process, without ever giving it any external indication that it's on the right track, is somehow able to increase its accuracy. Although researchers are able to quantify and tune this phenomenon, they don't really understand how it's possible that an LLM behaves this way. Somehow, purely statistical properties of natural language go an incredibly long way toward encoding correct mathematical reasoning. I'm actually surprised at how few people seem to acknowledge how "impossible" this empirical finding is. Most people are either in denial that it's true, or have been so dulled by familiarity that it no longer seems surprising, or try to cope by inventing some glib, and often inappropriately anthropomorphic, "explanation" even though they actually don't understand.

To get back to Lean, I would say that the attitude of the AI companies is understandable. They don't understand how the models seem to be getting close to AGI, and they don't know whether continuing down the same path they're currently following will lead to AGI. But they can observe what's happening empirically, and make heuristic predictions based on past performance. Under such circumstances, it's natural that they would continue to pursue strategies that have worked in the past (even if they fundamentally don't understand why those strategies work), until those strategies are proven to fail. Mathematics is small potatoes compared to their real goal of AGI, and so if Lean is needed only in certain special situations that are of interest only to professional mathematicians, then the AI labs are going to devote only a small fraction of their resources in that direction.

Ralf Stephan said:

Sorry no, this is no longer true since chain-of-thought

As far as I can see CoT doesn't have any bearing on "frontier models fundamentally being nothing more than (conditioned) (pseudo) randomized next-token generators".

A LLM using CoT or not using CoT generates tokens (pseudo) randomly from a prior that is conditioned on everything generated up until but not including the token being generated.

CoT simply encourages the LLM to take "smaller logical steps" when generating tokens.

We are veering off topic so this is my last incessant reply . But I do feel strongly about that .

I am not so sure I buy its reasoning though , like if you ask me 1000 times “1+1?” and I say “2” and why every time. But one time I randomly just say “67” , and when asked why I don’t even know myself why

Also I personally don’t believe CoT is at it seems either , or that it is reasoning too , because unlike reasoning there are times of wrong steps and randomly right answer , and right steps then randomly wrong answer .

My understanding is that it doesn't work like this any more: you don't randomly sample from all tokens, you make some kind of truncation to ensure that the nonsense 0.01% answer really never happens, rather than letting the machine talk nonsense every 10,000 tokens.
